name: Lena Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It starts with the hens, two thousand of them, free range on the slope behind the house. Then it's the vegetable beds, then the farm shop opens at ten and I'm behind the counter half the day talking to people about leeks. My husband Joaquim does the tractor work and the repairs, and we've got two hired hands, Marta and Kofi, who I'd trust with my life. We bought the place thirty years ago with a loan and a lot of nerve.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the shop, honestly, more than I expected. People come in and tell me about their grandchildren while I weigh their potatoes. What wears me out is egg prices. The big sheds down the motorway sell a dozen for less than it costs me to feed the birds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get on with the real problems, like what supermarkets pay farmers. I'd probably post something in the farm shop's newsletter about how the best tech we've got is still a good pair of boots. People like that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my worries stay the same old worries. Egg prices, weather, Joaquim's back. That's not nothing, but it's familiar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as we are. Maybe I'd use the chat program a little more for the newsletter and the shop's price lists, since that bit's proven useful. Otherwise we keep saving our bit each month, about three or four months of costs in the bank, and keep paying Marta and Kofi properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit flat, maybe, because I'd half hoped it might help with the dull stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools yourself at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. My daughter Clara set it up on my phone, and I use it to write the shop newsletter and to ask what a strange spot on a tomato leaf is. It's handy, but I always check with the neighbour who's been growing tomatoes for forty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So if this picture is how it goes, is there anything you'd still want to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The prices, always. I'd keep pushing our growers' group to sell together to the schools in town. That's a change that has nothing to do with computers.

S0.say: She'd say good, now let's deal with the real problems like supermarket prices, and post in her farm shop newsletter that the best tech is still a good pair of boots.
S0.think: Privately it means her worries stay the familiar ones: egg prices, weather and her husband's back, which aren't small but are known.
S0.do: Carries on as normal, using an AI chat tool a little more for the shop newsletter and price lists. Keeps saving monthly with three to four months of costs banked and keeps paying her two workers properly.
S0.feel: Calm, with a slight flatness because she'd hoped AI might take the dull jobs.
S0.quote: The best tech we've got is still a good pair of boots.
S0.fieldNote: Lena is practical and warm, and her real enemy is low prices, not technology. She uses AI lightly and checks it against a neighbour's experience, which is exactly her steady style. She keeps turning the conversation back to collective selling, which shows where her politics live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules so the change is shared out fairly, and that small farms get help to buy in, not just the big sheds. I'd say it at the growers' group and I'd sign the petitions. I'd also say, honestly, that some of these machines might save my husband's back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it'd be fine for us as owners, but it'd squeeze the people we employ. Our hens and vegetables would still need us, the shop still needs a face. It's Marta and Kofi I'd lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the neighbours had tried things, then go in with the growers' group on a shared weeding robot, maybe split five ways so it's a few thousand each. I'd use the AI more for the books. And I'd pay for Marta to do a course on running the machines, so she's the one with the skills and not the dealer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me so much as for the people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks on your farm could you see a machine taking over in those few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weeding, definitely. There are little robots now that go up and down the carrot rows and zap weeds with a laser. Egg collecting too, probably, and the books. Not the shop, I don't think, people want a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Marta and Kofi were people you'd trust with your life. What happens to them in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part I'd fight about. Marta's forty and sharp, she could learn the machines and run them for three or four farms. Kofi is sixty and his English isn't strong, and I don't see who'd retrain him, so I'd keep him on as long as the money lasts.

S1.say: She'd tell her growers' group and sign petitions saying the change must be shared fairly, with small farms helped to buy machines, while admitting they could save her husband's back.
S1.think: Privately she thinks owners like her would be fine, but the people they employ would be squeezed, and she'd lose sleep over her two hired hands.
S1.do: Waits for neighbours to prove the machines, then shares a weeding robot five ways through the growers' group at a few thousand each. Uses AI more for the books and pays for her younger worker to train on the machines.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly on behalf of the people around her rather than herself.
S1.quote: Kofi is sixty and his English isn't strong, and I don't see who'd retrain him, so I'd keep him on as long as the money lasts.
S1.fieldNote: Her progressive views show up as concrete care for named workers rather than slogans. The shared-robot plan is typical of someone who adopts once things are proven and prefers co-operation to going alone. She separates the two workers' prospects clearly and honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to hold the big firms to account and make them pay into something that looks after people. Publicly I'd be quite angry, I think. I'd be saying it's the people who grow our food who get thrown away first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the big egg sheds would go fully robotic and the price of a dozen would drop through the floor. Our shop sells on trust and faces, and I'm not sure trust pays the feed bill. We're fifty-eight, we haven't paid off the last tractor loan, and that frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop all spending on the farm that isn't feed and wages, including the new polytunnel we'd planned for next spring. I'd go with the growers' group to the regional council and push for emergency support for small farms and their workers. I'd ask our son Ivo whether he could help with the loan payments for a year if the shop slowed down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel like the ground had shifted while I was still standing on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very little time. What's the first bill or decision that would worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tractor loan. It's about four hundred a month for another three years, and with egg prices falling that's the one that would keep me up. After that, it's whether I can keep paying Marta and Kofi.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're an owner with land. Does that make you feel safer than a worker would?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer, yes, if I'm honest, because land doesn't vanish. But land doesn't pay you either, not unless you sell it, and I don't want to be the woman who sold the farm to a robot company. That would feel like losing an argument with the whole world.

S2.say: She'd angrily say in public that the government must hold big firms to account and make them fund support for people, because food growers get thrown away first.
S2.think: Privately she expects robotic egg sheds to crash prices, fears the shop's trust won't pay the feed bill, and is frightened by the unpaid tractor loan at fifty-eight.
S2.do: Halts all farm spending except feed and wages, including a planned polytunnel. Lobbies the regional council with her growers' group for emergency support, and asks her son for help with loan payments for a year.
S2.feel: Anxious, as if the ground had shifted while she was still standing on it.
S2.quote: I don't want to be the woman who sold the farm to a robot company.
S2.fieldNote: This is where the threat becomes financial for her, and the tractor loan is the concrete pressure point. She's honest that owning land makes her safer than her workers, which sits awkwardly with her politics. Asking her son for help is framed as practical, not shameful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a window and we should use it, and I'd keep saying it at every growers' meeting. Five years is enough to set up proper co-operatives that own the robots together. I'd be the one with the clipboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is the difference between being caught with the loan and being clear of it. I'd be sixty-three, the loan paid, and I could decide calmly whether to keep going. It's still fast, but I can see my way through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off the tractor loan early, putting the polytunnel money toward it this year. I'd help set up a machine co-operative with four or five neighbours and buy in once the first farms had used it for a season. And I'd talk to Marta about her taking on more of the farm, maybe a share in the egg business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with my sleeves rolled up. It's a worry I can do something with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to pay the loan off, time to watch other farms try things first, and time to look after Marta and Kofi properly. With two years I'm just bailing water. With five I'm steering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it's coming anyway, would you buy into the machines yourself this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, through the co-operative, once I'd seen it work for a season on someone else's farm. I'm not the first in line, but I'm not the last either. I'd want us to own the machine, not rent it from the company.

S3.say: She'd say at every growers' meeting that five years is a window to set up co-operatives that own robots together, and volunteer to organise it.
S3.think: Privately five years means clearing the tractor loan by sixty-three and being able to decide calmly whether to carry on, which makes it manageable.
S3.do: Pays the tractor loan off early using the polytunnel money. Helps set up a machine co-operative with four or five neighbours and buys in after a season of others' use, and offers her worker Marta a share in the egg business.
S3.feel: Uneasy but ready to act, a worry she can do something about.
S3.quote: With two years I'm just bailing water. With five I'm steering.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time lets her steady, proof-first approach work, and her mood drops accordingly. She returns to collective ownership as the answer, consistent with her politics. Offering her worker a share is a striking, concrete act of the fairness she talks about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this decently, so there's no excuse for doing it badly. I'd want public money for training farmworkers, starting now, not in year nine. I'd keep that line at the growers' group and in the newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully I think we'd be retired by then, or nearly. The question becomes who takes the farm on, and whether anyone wants a farm that robots can run. It makes me sad more than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd plan our retirement for around sixty-five and start handing over to Marta in stages over the next five years. We'd keep saving steadily and join the machine co-operative once it's proven. I'd use the AI for the succession paperwork, which I hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit sad. Not frightened, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years would take you and Joaquim to sixty-eight. How does that change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About sixty-five, I think, a bit earlier than we'd said before. Ten years is enough to hand over gently instead of all at once. Joaquim wants to fish, he's been saying so for twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about the farm in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the farm isn't their duty. Ivo teaches and Clara lives in the city, and they shouldn't feel guilty. If Marta wants it, and we can make it fair, that's a better ending than selling to a big firm.

S4.say: She'd say ten years leaves no excuse for doing this badly, and call for public money to train farmworkers starting now, repeating it at the growers' group and in her newsletter.
S4.think: Privately she expects to be retired or nearly, and the real question becomes who takes on a farm that robots can run, which makes her sad more than scared.
S4.do: Brings retirement forward to around sixty-five and hands the farm over to her worker Marta in stages over five years. Keeps saving and joins the machine co-operative once proven, using AI for succession paperwork.
S4.feel: Uneasy and a little sad about the farm's future, but not frightened.
S4.quote: Joaquim wants to fish, he's been saying so for twenty years.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, her concern turns to legacy rather than survival. Handing the farm to her worker instead of her children is a values choice that fits her outlook. The sadness here is quieter than the fear in the faster scenarios.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of the loan and because Marta and Kofi would have nowhere to go. What would help is grants for small farms to buy machines together, and a proper wage support scheme for farmworkers while they retrain. Not a loan, a grant.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the customers. If everyone's out of work, who buys eggs at my price? A robot can lay the egg, fine, but somebody still has to be able to pay for it.

headlineQuote: A robot can lay the egg, fine, but somebody still has to be able to pay for it.
portrait: Lena Silva, 58, runs a free-range egg and vegetable farm with a farm shop alongside her husband Joaquim and two hired hands. She's warm, practical and progressive, uses AI now and then for her newsletter, and adopts new machines only once neighbours have proved them. Her worries centre on egg prices, an unpaid tractor loan and her workers' futures. She is calm if AI fizzles and anxious if AGI comes in two years, but with five or ten years she turns to co-operative ownership and a staged handover to her worker Marta.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years worries her most, because of the outstanding tractor loan and because her two hired hands would have nowhere to go.
whatWouldHelp: Grants, not loans, for small farms to buy machines together, and a wage support scheme for farmworkers while they retrain.
